passage: The power had gone out at the warehouse, and the generator droned so loudly that Raghav had to shout over it. The truck was due in an hour. Meera, the supervisor, watched from her desk and said nothing. Two packers, Kabir and Sunil, slowed down to listen. Raghav held up the dispatch sheet. “Three times this week this changed after I signed it,” he said. “The drivers got wrong counts, and I looked careless. I'd like to hear how it looks from your side, Joseph.” Joseph's jaw tightened, then eased. “The client sends new numbers late at night. I didn't want to wake anyone.” Raghav nodded. “Then post it in the group, and I'll call the drivers.” Kabir and Sunil went back to loading.

qa.q: Who said nothing while Raghav spoke to Joseph?
qa.a: Meera, the supervisor, watched from her desk and said nothing.

qa.q: What might Joseph have been feeling when Joseph's jaw tightened and then eased?
qa.a: Joseph probably felt defensive at first, then relieved to explain that the client sends new numbers late at night and that waking anyone seemed wrong.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that helped the two reach a shared plan?
qa.a: Raghav named the problem, said how it affected the drivers and his own image, asked for Joseph's side, and agreed that revised numbers would go in the group first.

qa.q: What is it like for Meera to watch this exchange without stepping in?
qa.a: Meera may be leaving room for the two to settle it themselves. The packers slowing down to listen show that the whole floor was aware of it.

'Can we take five minutes before the client call?' Kalyani asked. Afreen looked up from her laptop. Rakesh, the third person on the project, kept typing.
'Sure. What's up?'
'Last night the deck changed at eleven, after I'd finished my part. I had to redo the numbers at midnight, and I came in today tired and a bit annoyed. I'm not saying you did it on purpose. What happened from your side?'
Afreen sighed. 'The client emailed me late. I thought if I didn't fix it right away, we'd look bad.'
'That makes sense. So what if late changes go in our group chat, and whoever is free picks them up?'
Rakesh stopped typing. 'I'm usually up late anyway. I'll take the night ones.'
Afreen laughed. 'Deal. And I'll forward the client mails instead of fixing them alone.'

qa.q: At what time did the deck change the night before?
qa.a: At eleven, after Kalyani had finished that part.

qa.q: How was Kalyani feeling about the late change, and how do we know?
qa.a: Kalyani felt tired and a bit annoyed after redoing the numbers at midnight, and says so plainly instead of blaming Afreen.

qa.q: Which part of Kalyani's approach helped most, and why?
qa.a: Stating the effect without accusing and then asking 'What happened from your side?'; it let Afreen explain and moved all three toward a shared fix.

qa.q: What is it like for Rakesh during the talk?
qa.a: Rakesh stays out of it at first, still typing, but once the talk turns to solutions Rakesh feels able to join and offers to take the late-night changes.

passage: Last term, three of us new teachers shared one projector, and Charu had it almost every day. Mona and Deepak grumbled about it at lunch, but never to Charu. I was tired of teaching my Class 8 map lesson on a chalkboard. So one Friday I said, 'Charu, can I talk about the projector? I've gone without it for three weeks, and I'm starting to feel frustrated and left out of planning. How does it look from your side?' She went red. 'I thought nobody else wanted it. No one ever said.' That stung, because she was partly right. We sat with the timetable and made a sign-up sheet for the staffroom door. Mona wrote her name on it first. I'm Vinita, and I still think about how close I came to just complaining at lunch forever.

qa.q: What did they make to share the projector?
qa.a: A sign-up sheet for the staffroom door.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when Vinita raised the projector, and what shows it?
qa.a: Charu was embarrassed and surprised; she went red and said she thought nobody else wanted it.

qa.q: What could Mona and Deepak learn from how Vinita handled this?
qa.a: Instead of grumbling at lunch, they could name the problem directly, say how it affects them and ask for the other person's view.

qa.q: How might Mona see the new sign-up sheet?
qa.a: Mona had only grumbled before, so she likely felt relieved to have a fair turn at last, which is why she wrote her name first.

grounding: A young teacher raises a shared-resource conflict by naming the issue and its effect, asking for the colleague's view and agreeing on a fair plan.

passage: Supervisor's note, Tuesday, packing floor. Friction between Ganga and Jeevan over the loading bay has been building for a week, and the rest of the shift has started taking sides. Tonight Ganga asked me to sit in while she spoke to him. She was calm and specific: 'When the pallets are left in bay two, I lose twenty minutes moving them, and I feel my work is invisible.' Then she asked, 'What's stopping you from clearing it?' Jeevan said the forklift is booked until ten, so he has nowhere to put them. Neither of us knew that. Ganga suggested bay four for the overflow, and Jeevan agreed as long as someone signs the log. Salim from the other crew offered to check the log at shift change. I will put the bay-four rule on the board tomorrow and review it with all three next Tuesday.

qa.q: Why couldn't Jeevan clear bay two?
qa.a: The forklift is booked until ten, so he had nowhere to put the pallets.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling about the pallets left in bay two?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and unseen, saying she lost twenty minutes moving them and felt her work was invisible.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that turned a week of friction into a fix?
qa.a: She named the specific problem and its effect on her, then asked what stopped Jeevan, which uncovered the forklift issue and led to the bay-four plan.

qa.q: How might the rest of the shift, who had been taking sides, be affected by tonight's talk?
qa.a: They see the conflict settled with a shared rule, so they no longer need to pick a side, and Salim even becomes part of the solution.

passage:
Monday, late.
Finally talked to Chaitanya about the client calls. For a month he's been booking them at 8 a.m. without asking, and I've been dragging in half-awake and snapping at everyone by noon.
I tried what Mira from the other team suggested: one fact, one feeling, one question. I said, "You've booked the last five calls at eight without checking with me. I end up rushed and irritable all day. What makes eight the best slot for you?"
He looked surprised. Turns out the client's team only overlaps with us early in the morning, so it was that or late evenings. I hadn't known. He hadn't known I was struggling.
We settled on eight on Tuesdays only, which I'll prep for the night before, and he'll check with me before booking anything else. Neelima, who shares the account, said she'd been wanting to ask the same thing.
Not a big win. But I'm not grinding my teeth tonight.
Saurabh

qa.q: How many calls had Chaitanya booked at eight without checking?
qa.a: The last five calls.

qa.q: How was Saurabh feeling before the talk?
qa.a: Saurabh felt irritable and resentful, dragging in half-awake and snapping at people by noon.

qa.q: Why did the "one fact, one feeling, one question" approach work?
qa.a: It named the issue without blame, said how it affected Saurabh, and invited Chaitanya's side, which revealed the real reason.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya seem to take Saurabh's words?
qa.a: Chaitanya looked surprised, having had no idea Saurabh was struggling, and was open to a shared fix.

grounding: Shows a colleague naming an issue, stating its effect and asking for the other's view, and reaching a shared solution without needing to win.
